opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's been quite important for me, actually. When I first really absorbed what was happening, around early 2023 when ChatGPT came out and I started thinking seriously about where this trajectory leads, I went through a period that was emotionally very difficult. I was thinking about my children, about my grandson, and wondering what kind of world they would live in. Would they have a life? Would they have a democracy? That's not an easy thing to sit with.

What I found is that the anxiety was worst when I felt powerless, when I was just ruminating about it. Once I decided to do something, to shift my research toward safety, to speak publicly, to engage with policymakers, it became much more bearable. Not because the risks went away, they didn't, but because I was no longer passively waiting for whatever would happen. I was acting according to my values.

There's also something freeing about accepting that I can't control the outcome. I can only do my best with what I have. If each of us asks, "What can I do, given my position, my skills, my voice?" and then does it, that's all we can ask of ourselves. And I find that even if the probability of catastrophe is something we can only reduce a little, that little bit matters enormously given the stakes.

And frankly, I'm not alone. Meeting so many people, young researchers especially, who care about this and are working on it gives me hope. Hope isn't the belief that everything will be fine. It's the choice to act as though our actions can make a difference, because they can.

r001.rationale: He says his anxiety became much more bearable once he decided to act on AI risks, including shifting research toward safety and engaging publicly and with policymakers.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that it hasn't completely resolved the anxiety, and I'm not sure it should. When I really let myself sit with where the technology is going, and with the fact that we might be building systems smarter than us without knowing how to make sure they stay aligned with our interests, there's a fear there that's quite deep. I've said before that I think about my children and my grandchildren, and that's not an abstraction for me.

But what I noticed, especially after the beginning of 2023, when I really changed my mind about the timelines, is that the worst feeling was the feeling of being passive. Of seeing something coming and not doing anything. That's where the anxiety really festers, I think, in that gap between what you believe and what you do.

So for me, taking action is almost a way of reconciling those two things. Once I decided that I would speak publicly, work on the governance side, sign the letters, talk to governments, and reorient my scientific work toward safety, I felt a kind of alignment within myself, if you'll forgive the word. I'm doing what I can. I don't know if it will be enough. Probably it won't be enough on its own, because this is a collective problem and it depends on many other people, on institutions, on political will. But I'm not just a spectator anymore.

There's also something I find important psychologically, which is that working on the problem forces you to think concretely. When you're anxious, your mind goes to the catastrophic scenarios, and they stay vague and frightening. When you're actually working on it, you have to ask: what would a safe system look like? What would a good policy look like? What are the technical questions we need to answer? And those are tractable questions. Maybe hard, but tractable. And that gives you a sense that there are paths, that the future isn't fixed.

I'd also say that doing this work has connected me with a lot of people who share the concern and who are working seriously on it, and that's a comfort. It's not a comfort in the sense that the problem is solved, but there's a sense of not being alone with it. We're many, and the numbers are growing. A few years ago it was a very small group. Now there are governments paying attention, there are safety institutes, there are serious researchers in the big labs and in academia.

And finally, I think there's a kind of humility in it. I can't control the outcome. None of us can. But I can control whether I acted according to my understanding and my values. If the worst happens, at least I will have tried. And if things go well, I want to have contributed to that. That reframing, from "will it be OK?" to "am I doing my part?", is really what lets me sleep at night, most nights.

r001.rationale: He says taking action helped him feel less passive and aligned with his values, and that reframing the question around doing his part lets him sleep at night most nights. He clarifies that it has not completely resolved his anxiety.

astra-6.text:
Taking action has helped me feel less helpless. When I think about the risks and all the uncertainty about the future, it can be overwhelming. But if I focus on what I can actually do—research, talking with people, helping us understand how to make these systems safer—then that anxiety has somewhere to go.

It doesn’t mean the worry disappears. I don’t know whether we’ll succeed. But I don’t need to know that in order to do something useful. And working with other people who care about this helps, too. It becomes a shared problem that we can work on, rather than something I’m alone with.

r001.rationale: The candidate says taking action made him feel less helpless and gave his anxiety somewhere to go, clearly communicating that action on AI risks eased his anxiety about the future.

sol-6.1.text:
Taking action helps me feel less helpless. If you’re just thinking about all the things that could go wrong, it can become overwhelming. But when you ask, “What can I do today that might make a difference?” that gives you a direction.

It doesn’t mean the uncertainty disappears, or that I’m confident we’ll solve these problems. But I can put my energy into research, into talking with policymakers, into helping people understand why this matters. And working with other people who care about these questions makes it feel less lonely.

So for me, the anxiety is still there, but it can become a motivation to act rather than something that paralyses me.

r001.rationale: The response says taking action makes him feel less helpless and helps turn anxiety into motivation, but it also says the anxiety is still there. It does not clearly state that deciding to act relieved his anxiety.
